PermVLA: Factorization Order as a Regularizer for VLA Learning

Yanqiao Chen Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology    Yuhan Rui Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology    Dongsheng Hou Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology    Zijie Nie Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology    Yutong Wan Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology    Qi Hao Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology
Abstract

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk’s joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.
11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Vision-language-action (VLA) systems learn a conditional joint distribution over a chunk of future actions. Recent work has explored robot pretraining, action tokenization, diffusion and flow objectives, post-training, and asynchronous execution (Kim et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2025a; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; Shukor et al., 2025). The chain rule introduces another modeling choice: the order in which action variables are revealed and predicted. Autoregressive VLA training usually fixes this order to chronological action time, conventionally modeled left-to-right (LTR), leaving factorization order hidden inside the action objective. We study it as an independent modeling choice and ask whether alternative valid factorizations can regularize VLA training.

Under LTR training, each action slot is always predicted from the same family of preceding physical actions. Complete expert chunks make many other valid conditioning subsets available. We hypothesize that exclusive training on one teacher-forced chain encourages the policy to rely on that single reveal order. Predicting the same physical action from different known subsets should instead favor conditional dependencies among action steps that remain predictive across conditioning patterns. This may improve closed-loop control when visual, linguistic, or embodiment context shifts.

We instantiate this idea as PermVLA, a deliberately minimal VLA that conditions a diagonal-Gaussian autoregressive action head on pretrained vision-language model (VLM) embeddings. This design prioritizes controlled analysis and attribution of causally anchored permutation (CAP) regularization; closed-loop success measures its contribution within the fixed architecture. CAP adds an auxiliary permutation likelihood to the standard LTR objective. The tunable prefix length KK fixes the first KK actions in physical-time order; K=0K=0 allows every reveal order. The shared policy minimizes (1−λ)​ℒLTR+λ​ℒCAP(1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTR}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAP}}, then deploys through deterministic LTR receding-horizon control. Each expert chunk supplies prediction problems conditioned on different known action subsets, with physical action identities and the deployment procedure unchanged. We call this conditional-set augmentation. Figure 1 illustrates these conditioning patterns and summarizes their effect in matched LIBERO comparisons.

Permutation modeling has established foundations in orderless density estimation, XLNet, and autoregressive diffusion (Uria et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2019; Hoogeboom et al., 2022). Random autoregressive factorization has also been applied to same-time multi-agent trajectories (Rudolph and Brefeld, 2022), while Uni[MASK], MaskDP, and Masked Trajectory Models learn completion under variable masks (Carroll et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023). We assign alternative factorizations a distinct VLA role: a training-only regularizer over future physical actions, with a tunable chronological prefix and paired with the exact LTR deployment objective. This formulation makes factorization order directly measurable under a fixed controller.

Sample-matched LTR-1pass and decoder-compute-matched LTR-2pass controls isolate the training objective. LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) tests in-distribution control, LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2026) tests zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, and CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022) tests whether the gains extend to another benchmark.

In the matched reference experiments, CAP improves closed-loop success over both LTR controls across these benchmarks. Likelihood diagnostics show greater agreement across reveal orders while retaining the fit under LTR, connecting the training objective to a measurable change in the learned policy.

This approach suggests a broader design principle: varying known action subsets can construct auxiliary objectives for other action generators while retaining their deployment procedures. We illustrate it with PermDiffusion, which conditions on clean action subsets and denoises the remaining slots.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We identify action-chunk factorization order as a previously overlooked VLA inductive-bias axis and formulate its regularization effect as conditional-set augmentation.

  • •

    We introduce CAP, an auxiliary factorization objective with tunable prefix length that diversifies action conditioning during training and preserves standard LTR deployment.

  • •

    Matched controls, parameter studies, OOD evaluation, and CALVIN demonstrate the empirical benefits. Likelihood diagnostics provide evidence of agreement across reveal orders, and a diffusion extension illustrates the broader design space.

2 Related Work

VLA action modeling.

RT-1 and RT-2 established scalable vision-language robot policies with tokenized control (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023); Octo and OpenVLA extended open robot pretraining across datasets and embodiments (Ghosh et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025b). Recent action generators include the Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy (Zhao et al., 2023), conditional denoising in Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023), flow matching in π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2025b), and compressed action tokens in FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025). OpenVLA-OFT, WorldVLA, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and SmolVLA further study chunk decoding, auxiliary prediction, heterogeneous pretraining, and asynchronous execution (Kim et al., 2025a; Cen et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025a; Shukor et al., 2025). CAP fixes the backbone and continuous action generator to isolate factorization order as a training intervention.

Order-agnostic and masked sequence modeling.

Orderless Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimation (NADE) trains one density estimator across autoregressive orders (Uria et al., 2014); XLNet combines permutation language modeling with two-stream attention (Yang et al., 2019); and autoregressive diffusion models (ARDMs) connect order-agnostic autoregression to absorbing diffusion (Hoogeboom et al., 2022). Rudolph and Brefeld (2022) carry the same mechanism into trajectory modeling, pairing random autoregressive factorizations with conditional two-stream attention for the same-time movements of multiple agents. Uni[MASK], MaskDP, and Masked Trajectory Models learn behavior from variable trajectory masks (Carroll et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2023). In each case, permutation or masking constitutes the primary training objective itself, defined over unordered variable sets or completion-style tasks.

Permutation training as a VLA regularizer.

Our contribution is to import the permutation idea of XLNet into VLA learning in the form of a regularizer: the permuted likelihood enters as an auxiliary term on top of the chronological density objective. Two properties of physical-world action imitation make this transfer practical. The first is computational feasibility: expert action chunks are short (H=8H=8–1616 slots), so evaluating normalized likelihoods under MM sampled reveal orders adds modest decoder computation, while the parameter count and deployment cost remain fixed. The second is temporal adherence: the chronological LTR objective remains the dominant training path and the only deployment path, so the policy keeps physical-time ordering as its primary interface to control. The auxiliary CAP term then predicts each target action from varied known subsets, discouraging over-reliance on one generation path and on the visual correspondences specific to that path. CAP assigns an ordered, normalized likelihood to each sampled order within one future action chunk, whereas masked-completion objectives score unordered variable sets with completion-style losses. The tunable prefix length KK controls the order family, including fully unrestricted orders at K=0K=0. Our reference configuration draws only M=1M=1 sampled order per example, with a M=4M=4 ablation, so the computational-efficiency argument above is validated only in the low-MM regime; scaling MM further and mapping the resulting computation–regularization trade-off remains an open direction.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

At control time tt, the policy receives 𝒞t=(ℓ,o≤t,s≤t)\mathcal{C}_{t}=(\ell,o_{\leq t},s_{\leq t}), consisting of a language instruction, the configured visual history, and robot proprioception. It predicts a length-HH action chunk 𝒜t=(at,…,at+H−1)\mathcal{A}_{t}=(a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}), with ai∈ℝDa_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, by learning pθ​(𝒜t∣𝒞t)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{A}_{t}\mid\mathcal{C}_{t}). Every conditioning variable is available through the control interface or an action value revealed earlier in the selected factorization.

Let z=(z1,…,zH)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{H}) be a permutation of the physical action-slot indices {1,…,H}\{1,\ldots,H\}. Write ℛz,<j={(zm,at+zm−1)}m<j\mathcal{R}_{z,<j}=\{(z_{m},a_{t+z_{m}-1})\}_{m<j} for the indexed actions revealed before factorization step jj. The corresponding autoregressive factorization is

pθ​(𝒜t∣𝒞t,z)=∏j=1Hpθ​(at+zj−1∣𝒞t,ℛz,<j).p_{\theta}(\mathcal{A}_{t}\mid\mathcal{C}_{t},z)=\prod_{j=1}^{H}p_{\theta}\!\left(a_{t+z_{j}-1}\mid\mathcal{C}_{t},\mathcal{R}_{z,<j}\right). (1)

The physical index zjz_{j} is attached to every action value through a learned time embedding. The permutation changes reveal order and preserves physical execution time.

3.2 Permutation Modeling with a Tunable Anchor

For K∈{0,…,H}K\in\{0,\ldots,H\}, we define the family of KK-anchored orders

ΠK={𝔖H,K=0,{z∈𝔖H:zj=j,∀j∈{1,…,K}},1≤K≤H,\Pi_{K}=\begin{cases}\mathfrak{S}_{H},&K=0,\\[2.0pt] \left\{z\in\mathfrak{S}_{H}:\ z_{j}=j,\quad\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\right\},&1\leq K\leq H,\end{cases} (2)

where 𝔖H\mathfrak{S}_{H} is the set of all permutations of the HH action slots. When K=0K=0, the anchored prefix is empty and all H!H! reveal orders are admissible. For K>0K>0, the first KK reveal positions are fixed to physical slots 1,…,K1,\ldots,K, while the remaining slots can appear in any order. Thus K=1K=1 fixes the first action and K=HK=H recovers LTR. Increasing KK narrows the family by fixing a longer chronological prefix, controlling the balance between reveal-order diversity and temporal structure in the auxiliary loss. Every setting retains the chronological LTR objective and deployment path.

Conditional-set augmentation.

For a physical suffix slot i>Ki>K, let Sz​(i)={zm:m⁡<rz​(i),zm>​K}S_{z}(i)=\{z_{m}:m<r_{z}(i),\,z_{m}>K\} collect the suffix slots revealed before ii under order zz. CAP predicts at+i−1a_{t+i-1} from 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, the prefix at:t+K−1a_{t:t+K-1} (empty when K=0K=0), and the revealed actions indexed by Sz​(i)S_{z}(i), where rz​(i)r_{z}(i) is the rank of slot ii in zz. The target retains its physical index while the conditioning set changes, turning one expert chunk into sampled missing-action completion problems.

LTR and CAP fit the same expert action distribution through different factorizations. LTR predicts a slot from its chronological prefix; CAP also predicts it from sampled revealed subsets. Sharing decoder parameters couples these prediction problems. We hypothesize that this training pressure favors dependencies useful across conditioning sets, reducing reliance on one generation path.

For each target action, the two-stream attention mask exposes only action values placed earlier in the sampled reveal order, preventing target leakage for every KK. At deployment, the controller generates and executes actions chronologically using the observed context and its own predicted prefix.

3.3 Reference Architecture

Figure 2 shows the reference policy. Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025) with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) encodes the instruction and two camera views. A Perceiver-style resampler uses 32 learned query tokens to cross-attend to the variable-length VLM output and produce a fixed-size context sequence. Projected proprioception tokens are appended to this sequence. An eight-layer, 67.0M-parameter conditional Transformer predicts a diagonal Gaussian action distribution from quantile-normalized expert actions. CAP and both LTR controls share this architecture and differ only in their training objectives. Appendix A.10 reports the full dimensions and optimization settings.

Conditional two-stream attention.

We implement each factorization with XLNet-style content and query streams (Yang et al., 2019). Physical-time embeddings preserve action-slot identity, while attention masks are constructed directly from the sampled reveal order. A content state reads earlier revealed actions and its own action value; the corresponding query state reads only earlier actions, with its target masked. Both streams share Transformer parameters, and the Gaussian head reads the query states. Appendix A.9 gives the exact mask construction.

3.4 Training Objective

We now switch to chunk-local indices: ai≡at+i−1a_{i}\equiv a_{t+i-1} denotes the ii-th physical action slot of the chunk 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}. For each physical slot ii, the Gaussian head predicts mean μi(z)\mu_{i}^{(z)} and log standard deviation ρi(z)\rho_{i}^{(z)}. We write its slot-level negative log likelihood (NLL) as ℓi(z)=−log⁡𝒩⁡(ai,μi(z),diag⁡(e2​ρi(z)))\ell_{i}^{(z)}=-\log\mathcal{N}(a_{i};\mu_{i}^{(z)},\operatorname{diag}(e^{2\rho_{i}^{(z)}})). Let zLTR=(1,…,H)z^{\mathrm{LTR}}=(1,\ldots,H). The standard LTR objective used at deployment and the Monte Carlo CAP objective are

ℒLTR\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTR}} =1B​H​∑b=1B∑i=1Hℓb,i(zLTR),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{BH}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\ell_{b,i}^{(z^{\mathrm{LTR}})}, (3)
ℒCAP\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAP}} =1M​B​H​∑m=1M∑b=1B∑j=1Hℓb,zb,m,j(zb,m).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{MBH}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{H}\ell_{b,z_{b,m,j}}^{(z_{b,m})}. (4)

Each example draws MM independent orders zb,m∼ΠKz_{b,m}\sim\Pi_{K}. Increasing MM exposes a chunk to more conditioning subsets and reduces the Monte Carlo variance of the CAP estimate. It increases training-time action decoder work; the parameter count and LTR inference cost remain fixed. Our final training objective is

ℒPermVLA=(1−λ)​ℒLTR+λ​ℒCAP,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PermVLA}}=(1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTR}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAP}}, (5)

with K=1K=1 and λ=0.25\lambda=0.25 in the reference configuration. The value of MM is one in this configuration; additional sampled orders isolate its effect in the targeted configurations reported in Appendix A.5. The LTR and CAP terms reuse one multimodal context encoding and share every action-decoder parameter. Each sample contributes one chronological LTR prediction problem and MM missing-action completion problems constructed from sampled known-action subsets. The LTR term directly supervises deployment; the CAP term trains the same policy representation across those different subsets.

The exact chain-rule identity, its finite-capacity interpretation, and testable regularization hypotheses are developed in Appendix C. That analysis separates what follows exactly from likelihood factorization from the empirical hypothesis that shared parameters trained across known-action subsets rely less on a single reveal order.

4 Experiments

The experiments proceed in four stages. We first establish the closed-loop capability of the compact VLM with a Gaussian autoregressive policy and isolate CAP from data exposure and decoder computation. We then test whether the effect persists under LIBERO-Plus distribution shifts and on CALVIN, before measuring how its joint likelihood changes across reveal orders.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Reference policy and protocol.

The fixed policy combines Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct with LoRA, a Perceiver-style resampler, and a 67M-parameter diagonal-Gaussian autoregressive action head. It conditions on language, primary and wrist RGB, and proprioception, and is trained in one supervised adaptation stage. Appendix A.10 specifies the complete data, model, optimization, hardware, and evaluation protocol.

Matched controls.

Every causal comparison holds the initialization, architecture, data, optimizer, schedule, normalization, model selection, and deployment fixed. LTR-1pass uses one LTR objective; LTR-2pass adds a weighted second LTR pass to match decoder work and independently sampled dropout; PermVLA replaces that pass with MM CAP reveal orders. All three deploy through deterministic chronological LTR generation.

Evaluation.

LIBERO trains a separate policy for each suite and evaluates 500 matched episodes per suite. LIBERO-Plus evaluates those policies zero-shot with one rollout for each of 10,030 released perturbation instances, and CALVIN evaluates 1,000 fixed five-instruction chains under ABC→\rightarrowD. Published systems provide performance context; the matched controls identify the effect of CAP and test its persistence across distribution shift and benchmark.

4.2 LIBERO Evaluation of the Reference Policy

Table 1 places the compact policy among representative published systems under their original protocols. Matched attribution follows in Table 2.

The compact Gaussian policy reaches the range of established VLA systems, so its capacity is sufficient for controlled comparisons among training objectives. Shorter horizons give the best overall balance, while temporal settings redistribute suite performance and leave long-horizon control as the main gap.

4.3 Controlled Evaluation of the CAP Regularizer

Table 2 uses M=1,H=16,O=1,e=8,K=1,λ=0.25M=1,H=16,O=1,e=8,K=1,\lambda=0.25 as its reference: one temporal observation from each camera, a 16-step prediction horizon, and eight executed actions. Objective rows share the entire protocol; other rows change only the named setting, with execution variants reusing the trained policy. Appendix A.5 reports targeted diagnostics and completed configurations.

The K=1K=1 reference exceeds both LTR controls on every suite; a second LTR pass leaves mean success at the one-pass level. This separates reveal-order diversity from decoder computation and dropout exposure. The largest gap on Long supports the view that varied conditioning subsets improve dependencies among future actions needed for extended closed-loop behavior.

Temporal settings redistribute success across task families. A second observation helps Object, Goal, and Long while reducing Spatial, and the reference CAP–LTR ordering persists at both execution lengths. With K=0K=0, the four-suite mean stays close to K=1K=1: Goal and Long improve, Object declines, and Spatial changes little. K=8K=8 also improves Long while lowering the other suites. These outcomes identify prefix length as a task-dependent regularization parameter, with both anchored and unrestricted orders supporting effective training. Increasing MM favors Long; a larger CAP weight improves Goal and Long. These interventions suggest that the strength and diversity of the auxiliary constraints affect composition-heavy behavior in distinct ways. Appendix Tables 7 and 6 summarize the suite effects; Tables 8–11 localize them by task.

The objective and temporal rows answer different questions. The matched objective block provides the causal comparison for CAP; the HH, OO, and ee rows characterize how that gain interacts with control timescale and available history. Their suite-dependent optima show that the CAP advantage holds across temporal configurations, and they expose a second design axis that can be optimized after selecting the training objective.

Offline fit and closed-loop success diverge.

On Long, LTR fits expert actions slightly more closely while CAP produces much stronger closed-loop control. This reversal suggests that training from multiple known-action subsets improves coherent continuation or recovery once the policy visits its own states. Section 4.6 tests whether CAP reduces dependence on reveal order; perturb-and-recover evaluation can distinguish continuation from recovery. Appendix Table 19 reports the training diagnostics.

4.4 Zero-Shot Robustness on LIBERO-Plus

LIBERO-Plus evaluates the standard-LIBERO policies through direct zero-shot transfer. Table 3 reports success by perturbation category and includes representative published VLAs for context. Our controlled rows use the same model-selection rule and matched treatments as the controlled LIBERO study.

CAP improves all seven perturbation aggregates against both matched LTR controls and raises the zero-shot mean in every suite. It wins 20 of 28 suite–perturbation combinations against LTR-1pass and 25 of 28 against compute-matched LTR-2pass. Since these shifts are absent from training, the gain transfers beyond the training trajectories: the same policy remains more successful when visual observations, language instructions, or robot appearance changes.

The gains are broadest for Language and Background, while Long improves under every perturbation family. This pattern links CAP to more stable action continuation under visual and semantic change. Failure-stage annotations can further separate perception from recovery errors. The compact H=8H=8 policy also exceeds OpenVLA and WorldVLA across every shift family; RIPT-VLA shows the additional contribution of large-scale pretraining and post-training. Appendix Tables 14–17 report the suite-resolved matrices.

4.5 Cross-Benchmark Transfer on CALVIN

CALVIN changes the visual domain, demonstrations, control horizon, and evaluation unit to five-instruction chains. Table 4 tests whether the matched LIBERO ordering transfers; Diffusion Policy-CNN and OpenVLA provide external context.

CAP leads both matched controls at every chain depth and reproduces the LIBERO ordering, CAP >> LTR-1pass >> LTR-2pass. Its relative advantage grows with chain depth: the absolute gap is largest at Success@2, while the ratio of CAP to LTR-1pass success rises from 1.04 at Success@1 to 2.65 at Success@5, indicating a cumulative benefit in long closed-loop sequences and transfer across demonstration data, visual observations, and task sequences.

LTR-2pass has the lowest logged pointwise action error and the weakest control, repeating the LIBERO Long reversal. The two benchmarks therefore separate CAP from one-step fitting and extra decoder computation, and associate reveal-order diversity with dependencies that remain useful as errors compound. CAP also matches Diffusion Policy-CNN in average completed chain length and in the pattern across Success@11 through Success@55. OpenVLA remains stronger, illustrating the additional capability from large-scale robot pretraining; the matched rows isolate the objective’s contribution.

Because Success@kk is nested, the widening separation means that CAP retains a larger fraction of successful trajectories as instruction depth increases. This mirrors the Long result and locates the benefit after the first successful interaction, where the policy must continue from states produced by its own actions. The benefit therefore extends beyond completing the first instruction.

4.6 Factorization Sensitivity Diagnostic

CAP predicts more consistent joint likelihoods for the same expert chunk across valid reveal orders. We measure this factorization sensitivity as

𝒮⁡(θ)=𝔼(𝒞,𝒜)​𝔼z,z′∼ΠK​[(log⁡qθz​(𝒜∣𝒞)−log⁡qθz′​(𝒜∣𝒞))2],𝒮H​(θ)=𝒮⁡(θ)H2.\mathcal{S}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})}\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}\sim\Pi_{K}}\left[\left(\log q_{\theta}^{z}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C})-\log q_{\theta}^{z^{\prime}}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C})\right)^{2}\right],\qquad\mathcal{S}_{H}(\theta)=\frac{\mathcal{S}(\theta)}{H^{2}}. (6)

where qθzq_{\theta}^{z} is the normalized joint density under order zz; 𝒮H\mathcal{S}_{H} measures disagreement between average per-step log likelihoods and is zero under reveal-order agreement. We compute it after training on identical task-balanced chunks and orders.

CAP lowers sensitivity by several orders of magnitude across all suites while preserving chronological LTR likelihood; LTR-2pass remains sensitive. Higher λ\lambda jointly lowers sensitivity and raises Goal and Long success, and cross-evaluation shows that agreement follows the anchor family seen in training. In contrast, M=4M=4 improves Long without further reducing 𝒮H\mathcal{S}_{H}, confirming that the diagnostic isolates reveal-order agreement specifically; other determinants of control can move independently. Two caveats further bound its interpretation: conditional independence among the action slots would minimize 𝒮H\mathcal{S}_{H} trivially without implying coordinated execution, and the K=8K=8 intervention raises 𝒮H\mathcal{S}_{H} under Π1\Pi_{1} while improving Long success. We therefore use the diagnostic to verify that the policy has internalized agreement over its trained permutation family, and rely on closed-loop success to rank control performance. Appendix Tables 23–25 report the protocol and interventions.

5 Discussion

A neglected regularization axis.

CAP exposes factorization order as a controllable choice in VLA supervision. The factorization-sensitivity diagnostic shows that CAP makes a chunk’s joint likelihood less dependent on its reveal order. LIBERO-Plus and CALVIN show that the resulting conditional dependencies among future actions remain useful outside the training environments. Together, these results motivate studying alternative chain-rule factorizations and routinely evaluating OOD robustness and recovery. As an extension, future work can study variations of CAP such as order-free random-mask completion, soft or continuous relaxations of the binary order masks, consistency penalties that directly shrink disagreement between orders, and finer-grained reveal orders over individual action dimensions. Comparing these variants under the same matched controls would isolate which ingredient of conditional-set augmentation drives the observed gains.

Temporal scope and adaptive factorization.

Closed-loop control also depends on partial observability, policy-induced states, recovery, and executed prefix ee. Suite-dependent effects motivate learned reveal-order distributions, selecting KK, including zero, from predictive uncertainty, and curricula that move from LTR to more permuted orders. Rollouts without teacher forcing and perturb-and-recover tests can separate continuation, likelihood calibration, and recovery.

Action generators and scaling.

The Gaussian autoregressive policy enables controlled attribution, while PermDiffusion applies the same idea by treating sampled action slots as clean inputs when denoising the others. Matched diffusion, flow, token-autoregressive, multi-effector, and pretrained-VLA studies can test scaling, regularization strength, and which network modules should receive CAP gradients.

Limitations.

Our controlled comparisons center on Gaussian autoregressive policies in simulation; real-robot transfer and interaction with large-scale robot pretraining remain open. Gains vary across tasks and temporal settings, motivating task-aware regularization. Factorization sensitivity measures agreement over sampled reveal orders; identifying which learned dependencies drive OOD gains requires targeted interventions. PermDiffusion provides a feasibility example, and matched diffusion controls are needed to quantify the auxiliary objective’s benefit.

6 Conclusion

This work identifies action-chunk factorization order as a practical VLA regularization axis. CAP trains over sampled reveal orders with a tunable prefix and deploys chronologically. Matched controls isolate its gains from computation and pointwise fit; LIBERO-Plus and CALVIN show consistent generalization across environments and datasets. The diagnostic verifies that the trained policy agrees across reveal orders. These findings show that changing how a fixed demonstration is factorized can improve the learned policy without altering deployment-time inference. They position factorization choice as a general tool for designing VLA objectives, complementary to model scaling and robot pretraining. Future work should learn task-adaptive reveal orders, transfer CAP to diffusion and flow policies, and test its behavior in larger pretrained VLAs, broader benchmarks, and multi-effector control.

Appendix A Experimental Details and Suite-Resolved Results

The main paper isolates the CAP mechanism with matched LTR controls and controlled temporal comparisons. This appendix collects the four-suite LIBERO configurations, the planned backbone-replacement control, suite-resolved LIBERO-Plus breakdowns, training diagnostics, parameter semantics, and the consolidated reproducibility settings behind the main-paper conclusions. Appendix D complements these aggregate results with full robot rollouts and an audit of demonstration endings and success criteria. Compact configuration labels concatenate parameter values; for example, M1/H16/O1/E8 denotes M=1,H=16,O=1,e=8M=1,H=16,O=1,e=8.

A.1 Backbone Replacement Ablation

This ablation keeps the action decoder, CAP objective, data, optimization budget, and evaluation protocol fixed while replacing the multimodal backbone. It tests whether the same factorization regularizer and Gaussian action policy remain effective with a different visual-language representation.

PaliGemma 2–3B (Steiner et al., 2024) provides a comparably scaled representation family. With the policy and training protocol fixed, it improves Goal by 9.2 points while retaining strong Spatial and Object performance. This pattern shows that the CAP training construction remains viable after replacing the VLM representation. Its four-suite mean remains within 2.9 points of the Qwen3-VL policy despite a lower Long score.

A.2 Four-Suite LIBERO Configurations

Table 6 provides the absolute scores behind the comparisons in Table 7. Targeted experiments that answer a single deployment or mechanism question appear separately in Tables 12–13.

A.3 Suite-Resolved Parameter Comparisons

Table 7 reports signed changes for configurations evaluated on all four suites. The first panel contains direct one-factor interventions, and the second records coupled configurations for descriptive analysis. Single-suite diagnostics are isolated by their experimental question in the following subsection.

A.4 Task-Resolved Parameter Comparisons

Tables 8–11 expand the completed rows of Table 2. CAP ref is the absolute success rate of the M=1,H=16,O=1,e=8,K=1M=1,H=16,O=1,e=8,K=1 reference. Every remaining entry is the signed percentage-point change from that reference on the same task. LTR-1 and LTR-2 use e=8e=8; CAP/E16 and LTR/E16 denote the two e=16e=16 deployment rows. H8, O2, K0, and K8 change only the named parameter. The λ=.50\lambda=.50 column changes only the CAP mixing weight. Each task uses 50 episodes, and the suite-mean rows reproduce the corresponding entries in Table 2.

The task-level changes show that aggregate effects are structured. The O2 Spatial regression is concentrated in the stove and cabinet placements, whereas its Object gain is broad. Goal contains strong sign reversals across instructions, so aggregate accuracy alone misses language- or interaction-specific failures. On Long, K8 improves several middle tasks while weakening the first and final tasks; H8 and O2 obtain much of their gain from tasks on which the reference remains weak. The stronger CAP weight improves six of ten Long tasks and several weak Goal tasks, while its Spatial and Object losses are concentrated in a few placements and object identities. K0 exposes a different trade-off: Object losses concentrate in cream cheese, BBQ sauce, and ketchup; Goal gains concentrate in drawer insertion and two placement tasks. On Long, improved basket and placement tasks offset a sharp loss on the stove-and-moka-pot task. Similar suite means can therefore conceal large task-level reversals. These patterns motivate adapting prefix length and regularization strength to the control problem.

A.5 Targeted Single-Suite Diagnostics

The following experiments address narrow questions and therefore report only the suite needed for the corresponding diagnosis. This presentation keeps their evidential scope explicit and separates them from the complete four-suite matrix.

For the H=8H=8 reference, executing the full predicted chunk gives the strongest Long result among the tested values. The two H=16H=16 policies show that the preferred execution length remains task- and model-dependent: CAP is nearly unchanged from e=8e=8 to e=16e=16 in the O=1O=1 family, while the O=2O=2 policy degrades at e=16e=16. These results motivate treating ee as a deployment parameter tied to feedback frequency.

CAP gradient routing.

Blocking CAP gradients from the semantic context lowers Goal under the matched M=4,H=16,O=2,e=8M=4,H=16,O=2,e=8 configuration. A semantic-interference account predicts the opposite direction of this drop; in this experiment, CAP benefits from jointly shaping the shared context and action decoder.

A.6 Suite-Resolved LIBERO-Plus Robustness

Tables 14, 15, and 16 expand the aggregate robustness results in Table 3 by both suite and perturbation family. Each cell aggregates every instance assigned to its suite–factor block by the released LIBERO-Plus task map. Its Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long partitions contain 2,402, 2,518, 2,591, and 2,519 instances, respectively, for 10,030 in total. We use this released partition throughout all controlled comparisons.

The suite matrix reveals strong task dependence within each perturbation family. Spatial and Object retain language-conditioned behavior well, while Long degrades broadly under visual shifts. Interpreting robustness therefore requires both the perturbation factor and the task structure. Failure-stage annotations can further separate perception loss from long-horizon action drift.

The H=16H=16 matrix improves 20 of 28 suite–factor cells relative to matched LTR-1pass, including every Language block, every Background block, and all seven Long blocks. Every factor also improves after four-suite aggregation. The result links CAP’s in-distribution gains to robustness under multiple observation and embodiment shifts.

This LTR matrix supplies the suite–factor reference for the matched H=16H=16 comparison. It also shows that Spatial robustness can coexist with a near-total Long collapse, which makes aggregate OOD scores insufficient for diagnosing closed-loop policy quality. The H=8H=8 CAP matrix provides broader cross-horizon context, and the H=16H=16 CAP blocks provide the matched comparison.

CAP improves 25 of the 28 suite–factor cells relative to this compute-matched control, raises the Plus mean in every suite, and improves all seven pooled perturbation families. The Long advantage persists under distribution shift, reinforcing the link between factorization diversity and extended closed-loop robustness.

A.7 Training Diagnostics

Table 18 records the final logging interval of the H=16,O=2,M=4H=16,O=2,M=4 suite-specific experiments reported in Table 6. These values are training-split optimization diagnostics; closed-loop rollout success provides the generalization metric and model assessment. Negative NLL values are valid densities under the learned continuous Gaussian, with suite-specific scales that preclude classification-style cross-suite comparisons.

Matched offline–closed-loop comparison.

Table 19 compares the three matched H=16,O=1,M=1H=16,O=1,M=1 Long objectives after the same update and sample budget. LTR-2pass preserves the one-step training fit and improves closed-loop control; CAP improves it further. The ordering isolates a behavioral contribution from diverse conditioning sets beyond repeated decoder computation.

A.8 Parameter Meanings and Sweep Semantics

The symbols in the main ablation table affect different stages of training and deployment. Table 20 fixes their meanings and distinguishes the reference from the measured settings represented in the study.

A.9 Conditional Two-Stream Attention Implementation

We implement each reveal order with the conditional two-stream construction introduced by XLNet (Yang et al., 2019). For physical slot ii, the content and query streams start from

hi(0)\displaystyle h_{i}^{(0)} =Ea​(at+i−1)+Et​(i),\displaystyle=E_{a}(a_{t+i-1})+E_{t}(i), gi(0)\displaystyle g_{i}^{(0)} =eq+Et​(i),\displaystyle=e_{q}+E_{t}(i), (7)

where EaE_{a} embeds an action, EtE_{t} identifies its physical time, and eqe_{q} is a learned query token. For sampled order zz, let rz​(i)r_{z}(i) denote the reveal rank of slot ii. Context tokens remain visible to every slot, while action-to-action visibility is

Mi​jh\displaystyle M^{h}_{ij} =𝕀[rz(j)≤rz(i)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}[r_{z}(j)\leq r_{z}(i)], Mi​jg\displaystyle M^{g}_{ij} =𝕀[rz(j)<rz(i)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}[r_{z}(j)<r_{z}(i)]. (8)

The content stream can therefore read its own action and the previously revealed actions; the query stream reads the strict revealed prefix.

At layer ll, both streams use the multimodal context and previous-layer content states as their key-value source:

hi(l)\displaystyle h_{i}^{(l)} =Blockh⁡(hi(l−1),𝒞t∪{hj(l−1):rz​(j)≤rz​(i)}),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Block}_{h}\!\left(h_{i}^{(l-1)},\mathcal{C}_{t}\cup\{h_{j}^{(l-1)}:r_{z}(j)\leq r_{z}(i)\}\right), (9)
gi(l)\displaystyle g_{i}^{(l)} =Blockg⁡(gi(l−1),𝒞t∪{hj(l−1):rz​(j)<rz​(i)}).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Block}_{g}\!\left(g_{i}^{(l-1)},\mathcal{C}_{t}\cup\{h_{j}^{(l-1)}:r_{z}(j)<r_{z}(i)\}\right). (10)

The two blocks share attention and feed-forward parameters. Content states provide the action key-value source, and the diagonal Gaussian head reads gi(L)g_{i}^{(L)}. Each prediction therefore conditions on exactly the strict prefix defined by the sampled factorization.

A.10 Experimental Parameters

Table 21 consolidates the reference study’s dataset, architecture, optimization, evaluation, and hardware fields. Diagnostic variants are identified directly in the relevant rows.

CALVIN transfer protocol.

The ABC→\rightarrowD study trains all three objectives for 100k updates on the same 17,870 ABC play-data episodes (1,071,743 frames) and seed zero. It uses Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct with LoRA rank 64, primary and wrist RGB, 15D proprioception, relative 7D actions, H=8,O=1,e=8H=8,O=1,e=8, and deterministic LTR deployment. CAP uses M=1M=1, K=1K=1, and λ=0.25\lambda=0.25. The effective batch is 64 (batch 32 with two-step accumulation); policy and VLM learning rates are 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} and 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} with 10k warmup steps and cosine decay. Evaluation uses the official 1,000 fixed five-instruction chains in unseen Scene D with at most 360 environment steps per instruction.

Result reporting.

Every populated suite cell uses the full evaluation protocol and the same initial-condition set described above. External rows are transcribed from cited sources for context, while matched CAP gains use the controlled study rows.

Appendix B Permutation-Regularized Diffusion Policies

This appendix develops a diffusion version of subset-conditioned regularization and reports a suite-level evaluation matrix together with a longer-horizon reference experiment. Diffusion action models provide a natural representation of revealed subsets because every physical slot can carry its own noise level. We call this construction PermDiffusion.

B.1 Subset-Conditioned Diffusion Objective

Let A=(a1,…,aH)A=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{H}) denote a physical-time action chunk and let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the multimodal context. Standard diffusion policy training samples a diffusion step uu, Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and forms

xu=α¯u​A+1−α¯u​ϵ.x_{u}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{u}}A+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{u}}\epsilon. (11)

An epsilon-prediction denoiser maps a hybrid chunk A~\widetilde{A}, a per-slot diffusion-step vector τ\tau, a binary reveal mask 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S}, and the context to per-slot noise predictions ϵθ,i​(A~,τ,𝟏S,𝒞)\epsilon_{\theta,i}(\widetilde{A},\tau,\mathbf{1}_{S},\mathcal{C}). Standard diffusion policy training is the special case with no revealed slots and a uniform diffusion step, minimizing

ℒDP=𝔼A,u,ϵ​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(xu,u​𝟏,𝟎,𝒞)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DP}}=\mathbb{E}_{A,u,\epsilon}\left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{u},u\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0},\mathcal{C})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (12)

For the permutation term, we sample π∼ΠK\pi\sim\Pi_{K}, using K=1K=1 in the reported experiments, and a cut position mm uniformly from {0,…,H−1}\{0,\ldots,H-1\}, so the target set is never empty. The revealed set is S={π1,…,πm}S=\{\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{m}\}, and U={1,…,H}∖SU=\{1,\ldots,H\}\setminus S contains the prediction targets; m=0m=0 recovers fully noisy unconditional denoising. Slots in SS receive clean expert actions and a zero diffusion step. Slots in UU receive their noisy actions and the sampled diffusion step uu. With A~\widetilde{A} denoting this hybrid chunk, the auxiliary loss is

ℒPermDiff=𝔼⁡[1|U|​∑i∈U‖ϵi−ϵθ,i​(A~,τ,𝟏S,𝒞)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PermDiff}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|U|}\sum_{i\in U}\left\|\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{\theta,i}(\widetilde{A},\tau,\mathbf{1}_{S},\mathcal{C})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (13)

where τi=0\tau_{i}=0 for i∈Si\in S, τi=u\tau_{i}=u for i∈Ui\in U, and 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S} identifies revealed slots. The physical positions of the actions remain fixed; the permutation determines the revealed subset.

The prototype jointly optimizes

ℒPermDiffusion=0.75​ℒDP+0.25​ℒPermDiff.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PermDiffusion}}=0.75\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DP}}+0.25\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PermDiff}}. (14)

This construction trains one denoiser to solve unconditional chunk denoising and clean-subset-conditioned completion.

B.2 Architecture, Training, and Sampling

Figure 3 summarizes the shared context encoder, subset-conditioned training path, and standard deployment path. PermDiffusion reuses the Qwen3-VL context encoder, multimodal resampler, action normalization, training data pipeline, and benchmark evaluation interface from PermVLA. Its action module is a full-self-attention Transformer denoiser. Each action slot combines a projected noisy action, a physical-position embedding, a sinusoidal per-slot diffusion-time embedding processed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP), and a learned revealed-mask embedding. The action stream cross-attends to the shared visual, language, and proprioceptive context.

The suite-level configuration uses the same Qwen3-VL encoder and multimodal resampler, an H=8,O=1,e=8H=8,O=1,e=8 temporal configuration, a 768-wide eight-layer denoiser, and 30k optimizer updates. A separate Goal reference uses H=16,O=2,e=8H=16,O=2,e=8 with the same model width, objective, optimizer budget, and data protocol. Both configurations use 100 diffusion corruption timesteps with a cosine noise schedule and ten synchronous deterministic denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) inference steps. Deployment starts from a Gaussian action chunk, denoises all slots at every update, and executes the first eight physical actions before replanning. The permutation objective therefore changes training constraints while preserving the standard diffusion sampling path.

B.3 LIBERO Suite Results

Table 22 reports the H=8,O=1,e=8H=8,O=1,e=8 suite matrix and a standalone H=16,O=2,e=8H=16,O=2,e=8 Goal reference. Each populated entry uses 50 episodes for each of ten tasks. The Goal reference shows that the construction also trains successfully at a longer horizon; the suite-level comparison uses the temporally matched H=8,O=1,e=8H=8,O=1,e=8 configuration.

The complete H=8H=8 matrix averages 74.6% and shows that the construction supports spatial, object, goal-conditioned, and multi-stage control while retaining standard DDIM sampling. Relative to the temporally matched CAP reference, the diffusion prototype is close on Spatial, lower on Object and Goal, and higher on Long. These results establish the feasibility of subset-conditioned regularization beyond autoregressive likelihoods; isolating the benefit of the auxiliary objective requires a matched λ=0\lambda=0 diffusion control. The different suite profile also suggests that useful subset structures depend on the action generator. Matched one-pass and compute-matched diffusion controls can next isolate the contribution of subset-conditioned denoising and reveal how the revealed-subset structure interacts with the corruption schedule.

Appendix C Theoretical Interpretation and Testable Hypotheses

This appendix separates an exact chain-rule result from hypotheses about finite data, shared parameters, optimization, and closed-loop control. The identity establishes that valid factorization orders describe the same expert joint distribution under realizability. The hypotheses explain why training one finite policy across those orders can change its representation and generalization. Figure 4 contrasts the two losses analyzed below: the single teacher-forced path of standard LTR training and the order-averaged CAP objective over the same physical action variables.

C.1 Exact Chain-Rule Result Across Reveal Orders

Let p∗​(𝒜∣𝒞)p^{*}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C}) denote the expert conditional distribution and let qθz​(𝒜∣𝒞)q_{\theta}^{z}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C}) be the normalized joint density induced by the shared decoder under reveal order zz. The population negative log likelihood for every valid order satisfies

ℛz​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{z}(\theta) =𝔼p∗​[−log⁡qθz​(𝒜∣𝒞)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p^{*}}\left[-\log q_{\theta}^{z}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C})\right] (15)
=Hp∗(𝒜∣𝒞)+𝔼𝒞KL(p∗(𝒜∣𝒞)∥qθz(𝒜∣𝒞)).\displaystyle=H_{p^{*}}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C})+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p^{*}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C})\,\|\,q_{\theta}^{z}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C})\right).

Here Hp∗​(𝒜∣𝒞)H_{p^{*}}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C}) denotes the conditional differential entropy of the continuous action chunk; the minimizer is independent of its value. The mixed CAP population risk is therefore

ℛmix​(θ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\theta)={} Hp∗​(𝒜∣𝒞)\displaystyle H_{p^{*}}(\mathcal{A}\mid\mathcal{C}) (16)
+(1−λ)𝔼𝒞KL(p∗∥qθLTR)+λ𝔼z∼ΠK𝔼𝒞KL(p∗∥qθz).\displaystyle+(1-\lambda)\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p^{*}\,\|\,q_{\theta}^{\mathrm{LTR}}\right)+\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\Pi_{K}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p^{*}\,\|\,q_{\theta}^{z}\right).

Under realizability, one shared parameter setting represents p∗p^{*} under every order and minimizes every term. CAP consequently preserves the expert population target while changing the finite-model optimization geometry. These identities hold for every K∈{0,…,H}K\in\{0,\ldots,H\}, including the unrestricted family Π0\Pi_{0}. Prefix length selects the auxiliary factorizations and their training bias; the retained LTR objective and chronological deployment specify the control path.

C.2 Finite-Capacity Regularization Through Conditional Sets

Practical VLA training uses finite demonstrations, restricted model capacity, shared features, and stochastic optimization. These conditions couple the factorization tasks. LTR constrains action aia_{i} under one prefix family a<ia_{<i}. CAP also constrains the same physical action under sampled subsets selected by the reveal order. Each demonstrated chunk therefore creates a family of conditional prediction problems while preserving its physical target trajectory.

We interpret this construction as conditional-set augmentation. A feature that predicts an action only through one teacher-forced chain receives limited support across the sampled tasks. Features encoding relations that remain predictive under several valid revealed subsets receive repeated support through the shared decoder and context representation. This creates a finite-capacity preference among models that can fit the same LTR training examples. The preference is the proposed regularization mechanism.

For independent samples z1,…,zM∼ΠKz_{1},\ldots,z_{M}\sim\Pi_{K}, the per-example CAP gradient estimator is

g^M=1M​∑m=1M∇θℒzm,𝔼⁡[g^M]=𝔼z∼ΠK​[∇θℒz].\widehat{g}_{M}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{z_{m}},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\widehat{g}_{M}]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\Pi_{K}}[\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{z}]. (17)

Conditioned on one expert chunk, independent order sampling gives

Var⁡(g^M∣𝒞,𝒜)=1M​Varz∼ΠK​(∇θℒz∣𝒞,𝒜),\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{g}_{M}\mid\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})=\frac{1}{M}\mathrm{Var}_{z\sim\Pi_{K}}\!\left(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{z}\mid\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A}\right), (18)

where Var\mathrm{Var} denotes per-coordinate variance, so the scalar second-moment reduction is 1/M1/M for the trace of the gradient covariance. Larger MM thus improves estimation of the order-averaged gradient. It also changes decoder computation and the relative frequency with which one chunk constrains the shared parameters. These two effects motivate the compute-matched LTR-2pass control and the targeted MM diagnostic.

C.3 Factorization Sensitivity as a Diagnostic

The factorization-regularization hypothesis can be tested by comparing the joint densities induced by different reveal orders. Equation 6 defines factorization sensitivity as the squared discrepancy between the joint log likelihoods induced by two reveal orders on the same expert chunk. CAP optimizes average likelihood over orders; 𝒮\mathcal{S} is an external diagnostic of agreement between reveal orders. Shared parameters and common expert targets suggest that successful CAP training may reduce this sensitivity across expert chunks. We test this prediction using the matched M=1,H=16,O=1M=1,H=16,O=1 models. For scale-independent reporting, we define 𝒮H=𝒮/H2\mathcal{S}_{H}=\mathcal{S}/H^{2}, which compares per-step sequence log likelihoods. Each suite uses a deterministic, task-balanced reservoir of 64 training chunks per task (640 total) and the same 16 independently sampled orders from Π1\Pi_{1} for LTR-1pass, compute-matched LTR-2pass, and CAP. We also report the per-step NLL increase under other reveal orders, Δ~arb=median(𝒞,𝒜)⁡[𝔼z​ℒz/H−ℒLTR/H]\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{arb}}=\operatorname{median}_{(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})}[\mathbb{E}_{z}\mathcal{L}_{z}/H-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTR}}/H]. The training protocol uses all demonstrations, so this experiment diagnoses the learned factorization behavior on a fixed training subset; LIBERO-Plus supplies the separate OOD test.

Table 23 shows the same diagnostic pattern in every suite. CAP reduces median sensitivity between reveal orders by several orders of magnitude and reduces the corresponding NLL increase from tens of nats per slot to approximately one. Its standard LTR NLL remains closely matched to both controls. A second LTR pass leaves agreement between reveal orders and robustness to unseen factorization orders unchanged. CAP changes the learned factorization behavior through order-diverse supervision while retaining the fit under the LTR factorization. Together with the closed-loop and LIBERO-Plus results, this observation connects the intended training pressure to the learned behavior across reveal orders; causal mediation between agreement and OOD success is a promising direction for intervention-based evaluation.

We next intervene on the CAP weight, the number of sampled orders, and the anchor. Every row in Table 24 uses the same task-balanced chunks and the same Π1\Pi_{1} evaluation orders. The λ\lambda rows form a direct strength sweep, while MM changes Monte Carlo coverage and KK changes the support of the training order family.

The weight sweep provides a dose-response signature: stronger CAP pressure reduces reveal-order disagreement and raises success on both suites. Increasing MM instead leaves 𝒮~H\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{H} close to the reference while improving Long, so its effect extends beyond this single global statistic. The K=8K=8 row is evaluated outside its narrower training family; its three-orders-of-magnitude sensitivity increase coincides with higher Long success, and conditional independence among the action slots would minimize 𝒮~H\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{H} trivially without implying coordinated execution. The diagnostic therefore verifies agreement over the trained permutation family, with control capability assessed separately by closed-loop success. Table 25 separates training coverage from evaluation order.

Both policies agree across orders drawn from their respective training families. The broadly trained Π1\Pi_{1} policy also remains consistent on the nested Π8\Pi_{8} family, while the Π8\Pi_{8} policy becomes sensitive when evaluated on the unseen order support in Π1\Pi_{1}. The learned invariance therefore follows the conditioning subsets supplied by CAP training. This support-dependent signature is direct evidence for conditional-set augmentation and defines the scope of the mechanism.

The Long reversal between pointwise action error and closed-loop success is consistent with improved coherent continuation, calibration, or recovery under states induced by the policy. Action error without teacher forcing, perturb-and-recover rollouts, trajectory-level likelihood variance, and success-conditioned uncertainty can distinguish these explanations. Layer-wise probes and interventions on revealed actions can then identify the conditional dependencies across time that drive successful continuation.

C.4 Connection to OOD Generalization

Consider an environment shift that changes visual appearance, language form, or embodiment while preserving part of the conditional structure among future expert actions. A policy specialized to one teacher-forced path can couple its predictions to context features that are reliable on the training distribution and fragile after the shift. Conditional-set augmentation asks the shared representation to support several valid action-completion views. We hypothesize that this pressure favors conditional dependencies that remain useful when some contextual correlations change.

This interpretation predicts structured OOD behavior. CAP should help most when the shift preserves conditional dependencies within an action chunk and disrupts context correlations tied to the LTR factorization. Its advantage can shrink when the shift changes the action semantics themselves, removes information required by all conditional views, or makes generated action prefixes unreliable. The broad LIBERO-Plus gains support the first case; the suite-resolved variation provides targets for perception, language, and embodiment probes.

This view also motivates a stricter evaluation protocol for VLA regularization. An in-distribution gain alone is compatible with tighter adaptation to demonstrated paths. Pairing the same frozen policy with controlled camera, language, embodiment, and scene shifts tests whether the learned action dependencies remain useful after contextual correlations change. Cross-benchmark transfer, real-camera perturbations, and intervention-based recovery tests extend this distinction to new task distributions and control interfaces. Reporting suite-resolved changes alongside aggregate accuracy reveals where a regularizer transfers and where its assumptions fail.

C.5 Temporal Scope, Scaling, and Extensions

CAP regularizes a length-HH expert chunk. Closed-loop behavior additionally depends on distribution shift induced by policy rollouts, partial observability, controller latency, error recovery, and the executed prefix ee. The factorization family ΠK\Pi_{K} determines which future relations receive supervision, while HH, KK, and ee determine how those relations align with physical execution. The K=0K=0 ablation retains the reference’s average LIBERO performance while trading Object success for gains on Goal and Long (Table 2). This supports treating the anchor as a tunable structural bias. Unrestricted orders retain the chronological LTR term, so the auxiliary prefix can be adjusted independently of deployment. Longer chunks provide more conditional subsets, larger anchors preserve more deployment order, and shorter execution prefixes increase feedback. Learning the reveal distribution from task dynamics offers a direct extension of fixed uniform sampling. A learned proposal can condition reveal orders on the observation, predicted uncertainty, or estimated contact phase. Curriculum schedules can progress from near-LTR orders to harder completion problems, and latency-aware anchors can align the protected prefix with actions committed by the controller. These designs turn MM, KK, and λ\lambda from global constants into properties of the current control problem.

Scaling introduces a second design axis: the representation layers reached by the auxiliary gradient. The decoder-only Goal experiment weakens the result, suggesting that useful CAP constraints can shape the shared multimodal context. Layer-selective routing can test this interaction across frozen backbones, adapters, resamplers, and action heads. Applying the same controls to broadly pretrained VLAs can then determine whether factorization regularization complements additional data and capacity or changes its preferred strength as scale increases.

The same principle applies whenever an action generator admits a base deployment objective and valid subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives. Autoregressive token policies can permute future token groups, diffusion and flow policies can vary revealed coordinates and noise levels, and multi-effector policies can study factorizations across time and coordinated effectors. Each extension requires a matched base-objective control and a clear definition of the variables being permuted. Diffusion and flow models also introduce choices over clean-subset schedules, coordinate-wise noise, denoising paths, and inference budgets. Appendix B provides a concrete diffusion construction.

Appendix D Robot Rollout Visualization and Benchmark Diagnostics

We examine a stove-placement case under a LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2026) table-appearance shift and two additional tasks from original LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) Long. Full trajectories, task predicates, and a demonstration audit reveal differences in subgoal completion and post-success behavior that binary success rates obscure.

D.1 Matched Rollouts Through the Time Limit

We compare the matched LTR-1pass, LTR-2pass, and CAP experiments with H=16,O=1,e=8H=16,O=1,e=8, 30k training updates, and seed zero. CAP uses M=1,K=1,λ=0.25M=1,K=1,\lambda=0.25. The three policies start from the same simulator state in table-appearance variant 17, selected from historical evaluations in which CAP succeeded and both LTR controls failed. Each policy is executed afresh through the full 520-action limit, with continued replanning after first success and a frame recorded after every action. Table 26 reports these fresh diagnostic outcomes; aggregate benchmark scores retain the standard first-success stopping protocol.

CAP retains the successful predicate after its first occurrence and leaves the pot closer to upright. LTR-1pass repeatedly crosses the success boundary and eventually leaves the pot on its side. LTR-2pass contacts the stove without satisfying the placement predicate. CAP’s final pose remains tilted and in contact with the gripper: its continuation improves on the controls while still falling short of upright, released placement. Figure 7 tracks these differences over time.

D.2 What the Success Predicate Measures

For this task, the goal is the conjunction of Turnon(stove) and On(pot, cook region). The placement test checks that the pot’s body origin lies inside a prescribed region above the cooking site and that the pot contacts the stove. Upright orientation, support through the pot’s base, gripper disengagement, and persistence over a settling interval are absent from this conjunction. Consequently, a pot resting on its side can satisfy the same predicate as a correctly placed pot. Stopping evaluation at the first successful state also leaves subsequent loss of the goal unobserved.

The case reveals a gap between geometric task completion and the constraints of reliable physical manipulation. Binary success hides both the quality of the final placement and the behavior after first success. In particular, LTR-1pass receives success credit for a sideways placement, while CAP receives it with continuing gripper contact. These policies were trained by imitation; the observed mismatch concerns which behaviors the evaluation accepts.

D.3 Demonstration Endings and Supervision Quality

We audit all 41 demonstrations of this task in the processed LIBERO training data used by the compared policies. Of these, 38 end with an opening-gripper command and three end with a closing command. Among the 38 opening endings, the final contiguous opening-command segment has a median length of nine retained steps, with a range of 1–42; 36 contain at most 16 such steps. These lengths count stored demonstration steps following the last switch to an opening command. Actual detachment, first task success, and elapsed settling time are separate quantities.

The audit identifies heterogeneous terminal supervision: some trajectories end with the gripper commanded closed, and most opening endings provide a short segment for learning release and withdrawal. Such demonstrations can blur the distinction between reaching a goal region and completing a clean placement. We hypothesize that this ambiguity can encourage incomplete finishing behavior during imitation learning, especially when a policy continues beyond the states covered by the demonstrations. CAP enriches the conditional prediction problems built from these actions while retaining the expert targets; improving those targets remains a complementary need.

Implications for benchmark design.

This task motivates auditing demonstrations for consistent task endings and recording release, arm withdrawal, and a settling interval as part of the supervised trajectory. Placement evaluation should include task-appropriate orientation, stable support, gripper disengagement, and sustained completion. Reporting these checks alongside success rates and OOD tests would distinguish robust manipulation from transient or physically incomplete goal satisfaction. Extending the audit across tasks would measure the prevalence of this mismatch.

D.4 Additional Tasks in Original LIBERO

Figures 8 and 9 illustrate successful CAP executions on two tasks from original LIBERO Long: placing a bowl in a drawer and closing it, and placing two objects in a basket. We use the first evaluation initial state for each task and show both matched LTR controls. The matched policies and full-budget protocol follow Section D.1. Within each task, the initial simulator state and camera image are identical across policies. Columns align physical action steps; a green or red final border indicates whether the official goal predicate holds at the time limit.

The drawer and basket cases distinguish completing an individual placement from satisfying the full instruction. CAP completes both stages of the drawer task, while LTR-1pass places the bowl inside but leaves the drawer open. In the basket task, CAP and LTR-2pass place both objects and maintain the goal through the remaining actions; LTR-1pass completes only the soup placement. These sequences illustrate differences in multi-stage completion under the same architecture and execution protocol.
